title: The Animals Sick of the Plague
text:
A plague swept through the animal kingdom. Not all died, but all were stricken. The lion called a council and proposed a remedy: heaven was punishing them for their sins, so the guiltiest among them should be sacrificed to appease it. To set an example, he would confess first. He had eaten many sheep, which had never done him any harm, and once or twice even the shepherd.

The fox hurried to reassure him. Eating sheep, that foolish rabble, was no sin, and it was an honor for them. As for the shepherd, he deserved it for claiming power over the animals. The courtiers applauded. Then the tiger, the bear and the other powerful beasts confessed their own deeds, and each was found to be practically a saint.

Last came the donkey. He admitted that once, passing a monks' meadow, hungry and tempted, he had eaten a strip of grass the width of his tongue. He had no right to it, he said. The assembly cried out against him. A wolf with some learning made a speech proving that this cursed animal was the source of all their troubles. Eating someone else's grass was a hideous crime. The donkey was put to death.

La Fontaine closes by saying that depending on whether you are powerful or wretched, the judgments of the court will make you white or black.
lesson: When an organization looks for someone to blame, notice whether the standard depends on the rank of the person judged. A fair process judges the act, not the actor.
people: The lion, the fox, the wolf, the donkey
source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book VII, Fable 1 (Les Animaux malades de la peste)
